title: Sterilization Indicators

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

summary: Physical, chemical, and biological indicators are used to verify that a sterilization cycle (e.g. autoclaving) actually achieved sterilizing conditions, rather than assuming it did based on the machine's cycle settings alone.
explanation: Physical indicators (gauges, printouts of time/temperature/pressure) confirm the cycle ran as programmed. Chemical indicators (e.g. autoclave tape that changes color, or indicator strips) confirm the load was exposed to the expected conditions, but do not by themselves confirm sterility. Biological indicators (spore strips/vials containing a known, resistant organism, typically a Geobacillus or Bacillus species depending on the sterilization method) are the most direct evidence, since they confirm that conditions were sufficient to kill highly resistant spores, and are the gold standard for periodic validation. Routine cycles commonly rely on physical and chemical indicators, with biological indicators used on a periodic validation schedule per facility SOP or applicable standard (e.g. AAMI/ISO guidance).

comparison.right: Does not confirm the load itself reached sterilizing conditions

comparison.left: Confirms exposure to expected conditions at the indicator's location
comparison.right: Not proof of sterility by itself

comparison.left: Confirms lethality against a known resistant spore challenge

commonMisconceptions: Assuming autoclave tape changing color means the load is sterile — it only confirms exposure to certain conditions, not lethality.
